content: Prophylactic administration of misoprostol is recommended at a dose of 200 mcg orally every six hours with food. If the higher dose is not well-tolerated, it may be reduced to 100 mcg every six hours. The final dose should be taken at bedtime, and therapy should continue for the duration of treatment. For FDA-approved dosage regimens, refer to the mifepristone (Mifeprex) drug monograph. For intravaginal use, an initial dose of 25 mcg (one-quarter of a 100-mcg oral tablet) may be administered, followed by repeated doses at intervals not exceeding three to six hours. Misoprostol should not be used in patients with a history of cesarean delivery or major uterine surgery. For prophylaxis following delivery, a single dose of 600 mcg orally within one minute of delivery is recommended. For treatment purposes, 800 mcg may be administered orally as a single dose, but caution is advised if a prophylactic dose has already been given and adverse effects are present. Misoprostol should only be used in settings where oxytocin is unavailable. Alternatively, a single 600-mcg dose may be administered buccally. In cases of intrauterine fetal death in the second or third trimester, where complete expulsion of the products of conception has not occurred, misoprostol may be used with caution. Patients with renal impairment should also use misoprostol cautiously, as peak plasma concentration, half-life, and bioavailability may be increased, though the clinical significance of these changes is unclear. For pediatric patients under eight years of age, the safety and efficacy of misoprostol have not been established. For those aged eight years and older, a dose of 100 mcg orally every six hours is recommended. To minimize the risk of diarrhea, dosing may begin at 100 mcg every six hours and increase by 100 mcg per day every three days until the desired dose is achieved. Antacids containing magnesium should be avoided or replaced with aluminumor calcium-containing antacids, as magnesium-containing antacids may reduce the bioavailability of misoprostol acid and exacerbate misoprostol-induced diarrhea. Misoprostol may also enhance the effects of oxytocin through pharmacodynamic synergy, particularly if administered less than four hours before initiating oxytocin. This combination should be avoided or replaced with alternative therapies. Common adverse effects of misoprostol include diarrhea (14–40%), abdominal pain (13–20%), and headache (2%). Serious adverse effects include anaphylaxis, anemia, cardiac dysrhythmias, chest pain, flatulence, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hearing loss, myocardial infarction, nausea, uterine rupture, thromboembolic disorders, and bacterial infections. Patients should seek immediate medical attention if excessive bleeding occurs. Misoprostol administration during pregnancy can result in abortion, premature birth, or birth defects. Uterine rupture has been reported when misoprostol is used to induce labor, with the risk increasing with advancing gestational age and prior uterine surgery, including cesarean delivery. Misoprostol is contraindicated in pregnant women for reducing the risk of NSAID-induced peptic ulcers. Patients should be warned of the risks of abortion and advised not to share the medication with others. Adequate contraception is required for women of childbearing age taking misoprostol. The drug may cause anaphylactic reactions, chills, and other adverse effects. Its safety in women with severe anemia is unknown. Misoprostol may cause birth defects, incomplete abortion, premature labor, or uterine rupture if administered to pregnant women. The safety and efficacy of misoprostol in patients with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal impairment, or respiratory disease have not been established. Caution is advised for women over 35 years of age or heavy smokers, as these populations were not included in clinical trials. Misoprostol is classified as pregnancy category X. During lactation, the drug is rapidly metabolized to misoprostol acid, which is biologically active and excreted in breast milk. Although no adverse effects in breastfeeding infants have been reported, caution is advised when administering misoprostol to breastfeeding women. Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E analogue that is rapidly de-esterified to its active metabolite, misoprostol acid. It replaces protective prostaglandins depleted by therapies that inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, inhibits gastric acid secretion, and protects the gastric mucosa. It may also reduce fat malabsorption in patients with significant fat malabsorption, potentially by stimulating duodenal bicarbonate production. The bioavailability of misoprostol is unquantified. Its onset of action for acid secretion inhibition occurs within two to three hours, with effects lasting at least three hours. Peak plasma levels of misoprostol acid are reached within 14 minutes, and the active metabolite is 80–90% protein-bound. Misoprostol undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, with urinary excretion accounting for 80% of elimination. The half-life of misoprostol acid is 20–40 minutes, and the drug is not dialyzable.
